name: Proportionality bias
statement: Proportionality bias is the tendency to infer that an event with large consequences must have had a large cause, offered as one reason conspiracy explanations appeal.
meaning: The claim is about a single inference, not about conspiracy theories as a class. A person learns how big an outcome was and reads the size of the cause off it, in cases where the outcome carries no information about the cause. Whether a computer crash cost a student his job, or whether a president survived the shot, is settled by things that happened after the event and cannot bear on what started it. Two literatures test this. One studies causal judgement directly and calls it consequence-cause matching or cause-effect magnitude correspondence, using diseases, plane faults, negotiations and tornadoes. Spina and colleagues file that work under the representativeness heuristic, entry 145. The other studies conspiracy belief and calls it the major event, major cause heuristic. The reasoning step is the same in both, and the results are not. The conspiracy literature also carries a second and much commoner measure, general belief in real conspiracy theories, scored from questionnaires about real plots. Evidence that a person who believes one plot believes others speaks to that measure and not to this one, because consequence size was never varied. Illusory pattern perception, treated under apophenia, entry 41, is a different claim again: it is about seeing structure in noise rather than about matching a cause to an outcome already known.

origin.who: Patrick J. Leman and Marco Cinnirella
origin.note: The paper that gave the idea its slogan. Its abstract, read from the Semantic Scholar record because no full text could be had, reports 64 participants reading one of four variations on a vignette about the assassination or attempted assassination of a hypothetical president, then rating how likely each of eight statements was. Endorsement of a conspiracy account was higher when the president died than when he survived. Levels of belief in real-world conspiracy theories did not relate to that inference, though high believers were more likely to doubt the reported details of the event. The earlier antecedent is McCauley and Jacques, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 1979. Neither paper's full text was obtained for this entry.

evidence: The largest reported effects are in the causal-judgement literature rather than the conspiracy one. Spina's 2009 Queen's University dissertation, published the following year with Ji, Guo, Zhang, Li and Fabrigar, gave 59 European-Canadian and 60 Chinese students a disease outbreak that either killed people or hospitalised them, followed by a highly infectious or a standard strain of bacteria. Participants tied the high-magnitude effect to the high-magnitude cause, 7.73 against 4.05 on a nine-point scale, and the low-magnitude effect to the low-magnitude cause, 6.82 against 3.72, an interaction of F(1, 115) = 160.18, p < .001, partial eta squared = .58. A negotiation scenario gave F(1, 140) = 133.36 and .49, and pictures of basketball players and tornadoes gave F(1, 134) = 50.20 and .27. Each of the three analyses also carries a three-way interaction with culture, .11, .13 and .05, with Canadians matching more strongly than Chinese. In the picture study that cultural gap rests on follow-up tests Spina himself calls marginal, at p < .07 and p < .09. LeBoeuf and Norton ran the consumer version. A computer crash was attributed to a worldwide virus rather than a cooling fan by 73% of participants when the student lost his job and 56% when he graduated on time, chi-square(1, N = 129) = 4.14, p = .04. A zoo disease was blamed on a bear rather than a rabbit by 36% against 20%, chi-square(1, N = 130) = 4.28, p = .04. Of the tests in their first set of experiments, the two conspiracy ones return the smallest chi-squares. An assassination in a small country was attributed to a conspiracy by 76% when war followed and 54% when peace did, chi-square(1, N = 74) = 3.80, p = .05, and a conceptual replication using the Kennedy assassination gave 75% against 64%, chi-square(1, N = 224) = 3.69, p = .055. A later experiment primed how predictable the world seems. Matching held among participants who first wrote about unpredictability, 43% against 18%, chi-square(1, N = 80) = 5.55, p = .02, and was no longer reliable among those who wrote about predictability, 51% against 43%, chi-square(1, N = 93) = 0.61, p = .44.

examples.tag: The power cut that emptied a district
examples.text: A fault leaves a whole district dark for a day, and residents assume something major failed at the substation. A loose connection can do the same. The scale of the disruption carries no information about the scale of the fault.

examples.tag: A place lost over a late form
examples.text: A student loses a university place because one form went in a day late, and looks for a deeper reason behind it. The consequence was heavy and the cause was clerical, and nothing requires the two to match in size.

examples.tag: The vote decided by a handful
examples.text: A referendum turns on a narrow margin and commentators reach at once for deep historical forces. A close result is equally compatible with small and accidental causes, which the weight of what follows cannot rule out.

replication.headline: The magnitude-matching inference reproduces across scenarios and two countries with large effects, while the conspiracy version of it holds in one of the four studies that varied or measured consequence size, and only among people asked to take the victims' side.
replication.detail: Van Prooijen and van Dijk ran five studies on consequence size and conspiracy belief. Study 1 gave 71 Dutch students a bogus report of an opposition leader in Benin who either died in a car crash or survived it. Conspiracy belief was higher after the death, 4.18 against 3.45 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 67) = 7.50, p < .01, omega squared = .08, and the authors read this as replicating LeBoeuf and Norton, Leman and Cinnirella, and McCauley and Jacques. The main effect was qualified by an interaction with perspective taking, F(1, 67) = 4.47, omega squared = .05: consequence size moved belief among participants told to take the perspective of Benin's citizens, F(1, 67) = 11.75, and not among those told to be objective, F < 1. In Study 2, with 79 participants and a shooting instead of a crash, the consequence-size term was flat, beta = .10, t(76) = 0.89, and only the interaction with perspective-taking ability reached the threshold, beta = .26, t(75) = 2.40. Study 3 measured perceived consequences of the 11 September attacks among 80 participants and again found nothing, beta = .08, t(77) = 0.69. Study 4, with 114 participants and a third perspective condition, reported the interaction, F(2, 108) = 4.02, and printed no consequence-size main effect at all; in the condition taking the perspective of the average Dutch citizen the means ran backwards, 4.18 after the death against 4.66 after the survival, F(1, 108) = 2.06, p = .15. Study 5 held consequences constant and does not test the claim. Nothing resembling a preregistered or multi-laboratory replication of the conspiracy result was located.

study.cite: van Prooijen, J.-W., & van Dijk, E. (2014). When consequence size predicts belief in conspiracy theories: The moderating role of perspective taking. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 55, 63-73.

limits: No effect sizes are printed in the structured fields. The two literatures report partial eta squared, omega squared and chi-squares on binary choices, and pairing any of them would invent a comparison no paper makes. The experimental base is also small. Every cell in the studies read here holds tens of people, and the conspiracy experiments turn on chi-squares of 3.69 and 3.80 in samples of 224 and 74. Three documents could not be obtained, all on 21 September 2026. McCauley and Jacques is described here only through van Prooijen and van Dijk, who report that its participants read about a man shooting at a president who either died or lived and were asked whether he acted alone or belonged to an organised group, and that suspicion of a conspiracy was higher when the president died. Leman and Cinnirella's 2007 paper was not read either, and its abstract was taken from the Semantic Scholar record rather than the publisher. Ebel-Lam, Fabrigar, MacDonald and Jones is described through Spina, who summarises it as a 2008 unpublished manuscript under a different title, so nothing here should be read as a report of the 2010 article. Two documents the previous audit called closed were opened this time. LeBoeuf and Norton's published article is posted in full by Harvard Business School, and every figure above now comes from it rather than from the 2010 draft. The accepted manuscript of Spina and colleagues sits in the University of Chichester repository, which Unpaywall does not record, and its figures match the dissertation's exactly. The search covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, PubMed, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar, and turned up no replication attempt indexed under proportionality bias, no registered report, and no meta-analysis of consequence size.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat the bias as an explanation of conspiracy belief in general. What the experiments manipulate is one inference about one vignette, made by students who mostly held no prior view of the event, and Leman and Cinnirella report that this inference was unrelated to how much a participant believed in real conspiracy theories. That last point is worth holding on to, because the conspiracy field's usual finding, that people who believe one plot believe others, is measured on scales that never vary consequence size and is not evidence for this claim. A second error is to quote the effect as settled. Of the four van Prooijen and van Dijk studies that varied or measured consequence size, one produced the plain effect, two produced nothing without a moderator, and one produced means running the wrong way, though not significantly, in the group asked to take the average Dutch citizen's perspective. The bias is also described as a human universal. Canadians in Spina's studies matched cause to effect more strongly than Chinese participants did in all three analyses, and both groups matched, so the finding is a difference in degree rather than a bias one culture lacks. LeBoeuf and Norton's own result cuts against permanence too, since a short writing task about a predictable world left the matching no longer reliable. It did not abolish it: 51% of those participants still chose the large cause after a large consequence against 43% after a small one. The Kennedy experiment is often retold as showing that people believe in a conspiracy when told the assassination prolonged the Vietnam War. The gap it reports is 75% against 64%, at p = .055, in what its authors call a conceptual replication rather than a separate experiment. Finally, proportionality bias and apophenia, entry 41, are run together in popular accounts. Pattern perception concerns finding structure in noise; this concerns sizing a cause to an outcome whose size is already known, and evidence for one does not carry to the other.

sources.text: Leman, P. J., & Cinnirella, M. (2007). A major event has a major cause: Evidence for the role of heuristics in reasoning about conspiracy theories. Social Psychological Review, 9(2), 18-28. Not read. The publisher's site at explore.bps.org.uk answered a Cloudflare interstitial with a 403 to both a plain and a browser user agent on 21 September 2026, which is a bot challenge and not a paywall. Royal Holloway's own research portal record holds no file, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex record no open copy. The abstract quoted on this page was read from the Semantic Scholar record for this DOI.

McCauley, C., & Jacques, S. (1979). The popularity of conspiracy theories of presidential assassination: A Bayesian analysis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(5), 637-644. Bibliographic record verified at Crossref. Not read: PsycNet returned an Imperva block page on 21 September 2026, Unpaywall and OpenAlex record no open copy, and this machine's egress refused every archive.org host. The study is described on this page only through van Prooijen and van Dijk (2014).

LeBoeuf, R. A., & Norton, M. I. (2012). Consequence-Cause Matching: Looking to the Consequences of Events to Infer Their Causes. Journal of Consumer Research, 39(1), 128-141. Published version read in full from the copy Harvard Business School posts at hbs.edu, which Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record as closed. Every LeBoeuf and Norton figure on this page comes from it. The authors' March 2010 draft, which an earlier audit used, reports a smaller version of the predictability experiment with different counts.

Spina, R. R. (2009). Cultural Differences in Expectations of a Correspondence in Magnitude between Events and their Causes. Doctoral thesis, Queen's University, Kingston. Full text read; checked against the accepted manuscript of the 2010 article, which reports the same figures.

Spina, R. R., Ji, L.-J., Guo, T., Zhang, Z., Li, Y., & Fabrigar, L. (2010). Cultural differences in the representativeness heuristic: expecting a correspondence in magnitude between cause and effect. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 36(5), 583-597. The published version of the dissertation below. The accepted manuscript was read in full at the University of Chichester repository, a location Unpaywall does not list, and its figures match the dissertation's exactly.

van Prooijen, J.-W., & van Dijk, E. (2014). When consequence size predicts belief in conspiracy theories: The moderating role of perspective taking. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 55, 63-73. The published article read in full from the author's copy at janwillemvanprooijen.com; the source for every figure in the replication field.

Ebel-Lam, A. P., Fabrigar, L. R., MacDonald, T. K., & Jones, S. (2010). Balancing Causes and Consequences: The Magnitude-Matching Principle in Explanations for Complex Social Events. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 32(4), 348-359. Not read: tandfonline.com answered a Cloudflare 403 to two user agents on 21 September 2026, and no repository copy is recorded. Named because Spina summarises its plane-crash scenario, but he cites it as a 2008 unpublished manuscript titled 'The Proportionality Principle in Explanations for Complex Social Events', so his summary may not describe the published article.

Leman, P. J., & Cinnirella, M. (2013). Beliefs in conspiracy theories and the need for cognitive closure. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 378. Full text read from the Frontiers PDF. It speaks to the neighbouring question, how need for closure and existing belief in conspiracy theories shape the reading of evidence, and it does not vary consequence size. It cites the 2007 heuristic three times without retesting it.
